newsitem.title: USA: April consumer spending gain lowest in seven months.
newsitem.headline: April consumer spending gain lowest in seven months.

text.p: Consumer spending edged up at its slowest rate in seven months during April, the Commerce Department said on Monday, kept in check by slim income gains in a fresh sign of slowing economic momentum.

Spending rose just 0.1 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $5.35 trillion after a revised 0.2 percent increase in March. Incomes from wages, salaries and all other sources were up an identical 0.1 percent to a rate of $6.75 trillion following a strong 0.6 percent rise in March.

Wall Street analysts had predicted that both spending and income would be flat in April, largely because of previous reports showing weak general retail sales and slower new-car sales that were only partly offset by a continuing rise in spending for services.
Nonetheless, saving stayed relatively strong at 5.1 cents out of each dollar earned during both March and April.
Commerce said the decline in earnings reflected a decline of $4.2 billion in private-sector wages and salaries during April after a $26-billion surge in March.
The government previously reported that 142,000 new jobs were created in April, as the economy continued expanding though at a slower pace than in the bomming first quarter.
"In April, average weekly hours and average hourly earnings declined, more than offsetting the effect of an increase in employment," Commerce said.
The Labor Department is scheduled to release employment figures for May on Friday amid expectations another 221,000 jobs were generated by the ongoing expansion.
Previously, the department said that March consumer spending had risen more robustly by 0.5 percent but it revised that down to a much smaller 0.2 percent gain.

Gains in personal income, which includes wages and salaries as well as income from sources such as dividends, interest and businesses, are essential for funding consumer purchases that fuel two-thirds of national economic activity.

Spending on durable goods, which includes cars, fell 1.6 percent to a rate of $646 billion during April -- the biggest monthly drop since a 2.9 percent plunge in September last year, the deaprtmentsaid.
Spending on nondurable products decreased 0.3 percent to a rate of $1.59 trillion. But spending for services was up 0.6 percent to $3.11 trillion in April.
Payrolls of manufacturing companies were up modestly to $700 billion from $699 billion in March.
